title: Musicians seeing the world; Budd Johnson in the Soviet Union
summary: Maxwell and Hinton reflect on growing up poor, and Budd Johnson prefers Mississippi to African revolutionaries' praise.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: That's one of the nice things about being a musician, isn't it?
We've really had some opportunities to see the world.

Yeah. Well, you know, I grew up looking at National Geographics, and things and dreaming. You know, you live in the middle of a desert, your father's out of work for four years, you don't think you're ever going to even get out of Tracy, little loan to these glamorous places like that. And the last few years, you know, I've been going to Nice every summer. And I don't do anything else, I've done more than I ever thought I would.

That's right, I feel the same way. I mean, being born in Mississippi, being black, I never in my wildest dreams have dreamed -- and yet, I thought that we were poor by the standards of America, blacks in Mississippi in 1910 when I was born, we were really poor. But man, I've been in some countries of the world where we, by their standards, were

Yeah, that's what Budd Johnson was saying. The last time we were in the Soviet Union, Bud was there. And we were in a foreigners dining room and some African revolutionaries came up. They had outfits and everything and gave the Communist salute and started calling him "Brother" and how did he like it when he was in the land of freedom, and so forth. Budd looked at them and said, "Man, I would rather be back in Mississippi starving."
He said, "You've got to be kidding."
